title: Iterators
learningGoals: explain what iter() and next() do
see how a for loop uses an iterator

youtube.title: Python Iterators: How a for Loop Really Works | Python Programming EP 73
youtube.description: In this episode you will explain what iter() and next() do, see how a for loop uses an iterator and write a class with __iter__ and __next__, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 One at a time · 0:59 A for loop by hand · 1:39 The list and its iterator · 2:09 Second program · 3:09 Recap · 3:42 Bug of the Day · 4:30 Challenge · 4:50 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Every for loop you have written secretly uses an iterator. Today we open the box.

scenes.onScreen: "One at a time": three numbered lines (1. iter(x) gives an iterator; 2. next(it) gives the next item; 3. StopIteration means: no more) and an analogy card: a ticket machine: each press gives you the next ticket, until the roll is empty
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: An iterable is anything you can loop over, such as a list or a string. The iter function turns it into an iterator, which hands out items one at a time. Each call to next gives the next item. When there are no more, Python raises a StopIteration, and the for loop quietly stops. Think of a ticket machine. Each press gives you the next ticket, until the roll is empty. And once the roll is empty, it stays empty.

analogy.title: Think of it like this
analogy.body: a ticket machine: each press gives you the next ticket, until the roll is empty

scenes.onScreen: manual.py: iter and next, one step at a time
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A list of three numbers. [HL 2] The iter function gives us an iterator, tied to it. [HL 3] Next gives the first item. Ten. [HL 4] The second. Twenty. [HL 5] The third. Thirty. [HL 6] Now the roll is empty. [HL 7] Next raises a StopIteration. [HL 8] We catch it, and print, no more. A for loop does exactly this, and catches the StopIteration for you.

code.source:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
it = iter(nums)
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
try:
    print(next(it))
except StopIteration:
    print("no more")

scenes.onScreen: The name nums tied to a list; the name it tied to a separate list iterator that remembers its place
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The name nums is tied to the list. The name it is tied to a different object, a list iterator. The iterator does not copy the list. It points at it, and remembers how far it has walked. The list stays the same. Only the iterator moves forward.

scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A Countdown class. [HL 2] Init remembers where to start. [HL 5] Dunder iter returns the iterator. Here, the object itself. [HL 8] Dunder next hands out the next value. [HL 9] When we reach zero, [HL 10] raise StopIteration. [HL 11] Otherwise, keep the current value. [HL 12] Count down by one. [HL 13] And return it. [HL 15] A for loop uses the class like a list. [HL 16] Three, two, one. [HL 17] List can also consume an iterator. Five, four, three, two, one.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as countdown dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, countdown dot py. 10, 20, 30, no more. Then 3, 2, 1, and the list 5 to 1.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: iter of x gives an iterator. Next of it gives the next item. Two: StopIteration means there is nothing left. Three: A for loop calls iter once, then next again and again. Four: Your own class needs dunder iter and dunder next. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

lines: Iter(x) gives an iterator; next(it) gives the next item.
StopIteration means there is nothing left.
A for loop calls iter once, then next again and again.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: an iterator is used up after one loop
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We sum the iterator twice. The first sum gives six. The second gives zero, with no error. The iterator was used up by the first sum. It never rewinds. Keep the data in a list, and every loop gets a fresh iterator. Or call iter again.

props.why: An iterator walks forward once and never rewinds. After the first loop it is empty. A list creates a fresh iterator every time you loop over it.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the iterator go home early? It had nothing next to do.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the iterator go home early? It had nothing next to do.
